name: Nikhil Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ha, there's no normal, but I'll try. I buy wine, spirits and soft drinks for Harlow and Pike, a drinks distributor that supplies about 600 bars, restaurants and corner shops. Mornings I'm on the phone to importers, sorting out which vintage is short or which brand wants a bigger order. I also taste a fair bit, which people think is the perk but it's actually the job. I love the people side, the importers who've known me ten years. What wears me out is the pricing games. Everyone's bluffing about stock and I'm the one who has to read through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, and I've used it a bit already, so I'm not disappointed. At work I'd say keep the tools we've got, no big new projects. To friends I'd say beware anyone who says a computer can taste wine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means more of the same, which is fine. I use an assistant now and then to draft supplier emails and check a price list, and it saves me a little time. My job's safe. What bugs me is the cost of living and what the supermarkets are doing to bars' margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the tool for the dull emails and the price list comparisons. I'd leave the importer calls to me. And I'd try to get to the next tasting trip in Portugal, because those relationships are everything. Maybe I'd put a bit more into our children's savings accounts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. There's the usual noise, but nothing sets it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with an extra hour a week if a tool saved it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it on importers. Over lunch, on the phone, in person. The best buys I've made came from a friendly chat with an importer, not from a price list. An extra hour a week is another coffee with someone who might call me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Marta works in HR at a hospital group. Does that matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's job in HR is paperwork and meetings, so if AI does take routine tasks, hers feels it before mine. In a plateau, that's not much of a worry. But I always keep it in the back of my mind, because two desk jobs in one household is a risk.

say: Beware anyone who says a computer can **taste wine**.
Keep the tools we've got, with **no big** new projects.
think: My job is **safe**, and the worry is margins and the cost of living.
With two **desk** jobs in our house, I always keep a small worry in the back of my mind.
do: Use the assistant for **dull emails** and price lists, and leave importer calls to me.
Get to the Portugal **tasting trip** and add to the children's savings.
feel: Pretty **steady**, with the usual background noise.
S0.quote: The best buys I've made came from a friendly chat with an importer, not from a price list.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **steady** style shows in using a tool for dull jobs only after it proved useful.
He notes Marta's **desk** job, a small but real source of worry even in a plateau.

steps.text: Use the assistant for supplier emails and price comparisons
Go on the Portugal tasting trip with the importers
Add to Arlo and Sofia's savings accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's pilot it on the dull parts and see. To friends I'd say it's real, but I've seen hype before, so I'll judge by results. Online I'd keep quiet, it's too heated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's real this time. Price comparison, demand forecasts, reorder drafts: software will do those well within a couple of years, and my team of six will need to shrink to three or four through not replacing people. I'd still be needed for the importer side, but I'm not as sure of my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, but only once the pilot proves them. I'd volunteer for it, so I'm in the room when they decide how it's used. I'd move a bit more of my time to the relationship side, importers and key bars. And Marta and I would sit down and look at our money, because both our desks are in the line of fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Interested and a bit tense. It's a lot to take in over a few years, and it affects us at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your buying could software do well, and where does it fall down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software does well on anything with a number in it, and it falls down on taste, on trust and on knowing that an importer who's gone quiet is in trouble. A bar owner doesn't want a bot, either. They want me telling them what's new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marta's workplace change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's hospital group will use it for rosters, recruitment screening and the like, which is her work. They'll say it frees time for the human side of HR, and some of it will. But she's worried about her team being cut by a third.

say: Let's **pilot** it on the dull parts and judge by results.
I've seen hype before, so I'll wait for **proof**.
think: It's **real** this time, and my team of six could drop to three or four.
Both our desks, mine and Marta's, are in the **line of fire**.
do: Volunteer for the **pilot** so I'm in the room when decisions are made.
Spend more time on **importers** and key bars, and review our money with Marta.
feel: **Interested** and a bit tense, because it affects us at home.
S1.quote: Software does well on anything with a number in it, and it falls down on taste, on trust and on knowing that an importer who's gone quiet is in trouble.
fieldNote: Nikhil is **steady**: he adopts a tool when the pilot proves it and volunteers to shape it.
Marta's job in **HR** adds to his concern, since both incomes sit at desks.

steps.text: Volunteer for the buying-tool pilot at Harlow and Pike
Spend more time with importers and key bars
Review our household money with Marta

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk about this right now, honestly, with a plan. To friends I'd say stay calm but move. Online I'd say that governments should be on this today, and make companies pay in for the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. This is the one that hits both of us. My buying and Marta's HR work are exactly the thinking work AGI does, and in two years nobody's ready. I'd be really worried that we're both out within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by cutting. The holiday goes, the car stays, no more drinks on the company. I'd put all spare cash in the safe account and ask the bank about the mortgage options. Then I'd ask the firm what role they see for me. And I'd talk to Marta about which of us retrains first, since the robots take about three years longer to come for hands-on work, so a trade for one of us isn't crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. There's no other word for it. I'd probably not sleep for a week. I'd keep a brave face for the kids, but I'd feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marta's desk job and yours both go first. What would you say to her that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta that we're a team, and we've got savings for about a year, maybe more if we cut. I'd say let's decide now what we do, not in a panic later. I'd say I'm scared, and so should she be, and we'll do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from if both of you were out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings: about nine months of spending, plus a bit in shares. After that, it's whatever we can sell, and the mortgage is the thing. We'd have to rent out a room, maybe. I'd rather talk about that now than at midnight with a letter from the bank.

say: We need to talk about this **right now**, honestly, with a plan.
Governments should be on this today and make companies **pay in**.
think: This hits **both** of us: my buying and Marta's HR are exactly the thinking work AGI does.
I'm frightened that we're **both out** within a few years.
do: Cut the **holiday** and company drinks, and put all spare cash in the safe account.
Ask my firm what role it sees for me, and decide with Marta who **retrains** first.
feel: **Alarmed**, sick, and keeping a brave face for the kids.
S2.quote: My buying and Marta's HR work are exactly the thinking work AGI does, and in two years nobody's ready.
fieldNote: Two **exposed** desk incomes is the central fact for Nikhil, and it pushes him to alarmed.
He'd want a **joint** plan with Marta, including a hands-on retraining for one of them.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and put all spare cash in savings
Ask the bank about mortgage options
Ask my firm what role it sees for me
Decide with Marta which of us retrains in a trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's get ready, properly. To friends I'd say it's coming, and five years is enough to plan. Online I'd say we need retraining and benefits that fit, and companies should fund their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the difference between panic and a plan. I'd still be afraid, but I think Marta and I could manage it. I'm good at relationships, and I'd rather move into something where it matters, like running key accounts or setting up my own small distribution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in supply chain or business management. Marta would do something in occupational health or counselling, something that requires a human. We'd pay off a chunk of the mortgage with the bonus. I'd use the AI tools more and get good at them, so I'm useful for the time I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan to hold. I'd say a bit like training for a race I don't want to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, we'd be firefighting. Five years, we could actually retrain, and not on a panic budget. We could save a third of our pay. It changes the whole feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you rely on if things went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's sister lives nearby and so do my parents, so family would help with the kids if we had to. Our friends from the school gate too. I'd also lean on the industry: I know people at other distributors, and I'd ask about roles.

say: Let's get ready **properly**, because it's coming and five years is enough to plan.
Companies should **fund** their share of retraining.
think: Five years is the difference between **panic** and a plan.
I'd rather move into **relationships**, like key accounts or my own small distribution.
do: Take a **supply chain** or business course while Marta trains in occupational health.
Pay off a chunk of the mortgage with the **bonus**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan to hold, like training for a race I don't want to run.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between panic and a plan.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **plan** includes Marta, which makes five years feel manageable but not safe.
He leans on **family** and industry contacts, showing a social support network.

steps.text: Take an evening business course in supply chain
Put the bonus on the mortgage each year
Ask contacts at other distributors about roles
Get good at the buying tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, there's time, let's use it well. To friends I'd say learn something, anything. Online I'd say stop shouting and start building retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a long time, and a lot changes. I'll be 53 and Marta 51. We have time to move, retrain and save. I'm not afraid of it, but I'm aware that I can't wait for someone to tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, use the tools more as they get proven, and pay down the mortgage steadily. I'd start building my own small business in specialist drinks on the side, maybe selling to restaurants I know. And I'd get involved at the children's school, since the community is a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, I think. It's something I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids Arlo and Sofia over the next ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Arlo and Sofia to learn to be curious and good with people. Do things where you have to show up. If they like cooking, or building, or caring, great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make it feel like someone else's problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. It's easy to put off. So we'd put a date in our calendar every year to look at it again, me and Marta over a bottle of something nice.

say: There's **time**, so let's use it well.
Stop shouting and start building **retraining**, because ten years is not forever.
think: At 53 and 51 we have time to **move**, retrain and save.
I can't wait for someone to **tell me**.
do: Use tools as they're proven and pay down the **mortgage** steadily.
Build a small **specialist drinks** business on the side.
feel: Fairly **calm**, because it's something I can plan.
S4.quote: We'd put a date in our calendar every year to look at it again, me and Marta over a bottle of something nice.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **calm** comes from time, not from thinking AI is harmless.
He keeps an annual **check-in** with Marta over a bottle of something nice, a steady and practical habit.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage steadily over ten years
Start a small specialist drinks sideline for restaurants
Use buying tools as they get proven
Steer Arlo and Sofia towards work that needs people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Marta's job and mine are desk work and they'd go together. What would help is a real income buffer for families where both earners are hit, retraining that pays you while you learn, and companies saying early what they plan. A bit of warning is a gift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think wholesale buyers are fine because we earn well. We do, but a mortgage and two desk jobs in one house is a fragile thing.

headlineQuote: A mortgage and two desk jobs in one house is a fragile thing.
portrait: Nikhil is a 43-year-old senior **drinks buyer** at Harlow and Pike, with a partner in HR, two children and a mortgage.
He is centrist and **steady**: he uses an assistant now and then and joins pilots once they prove themselves.
His mood climbs to **alarmed** when AGI is two years away, because both household incomes sit at desks.
He leans on **relationships**, family and a joint plan with Marta, and sets an annual check-in.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because his job and Marta's HR job would both go together.
whatWouldHelp: An **income buffer** for two-desk households, retraining that pays while you learn, and early warning from employers.
